sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Application security interview questions cover the OWASP top issues every senior backend engineer is expected to know — injection (SQL, command), broken authentication and session management, XSS and CSRF, insecure deserialization, dependency vulnerabilities (CVE triage, Log4Shell-grade incidents), secrets management, secure password storage (bcrypt/argon2), TLS basics, and the secure-by-default patterns in modern Spring Boot. Pair this with the Spring Security page for the auth-specific surface.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Defence in depth, with the **OWASP Top 10** as the default threat catalogue:

- **Injection** — parameterised queries, prepared statements.
- **AuthN / AuthZ** — strong password storage (BCrypt / Argon2), least privilege.
- **XSS / CSRF** — output encoding, CSRF tokens for cookie auth.
- **Crypto at rest + in transit** — TLS 1.2+, AES-GCM.
- **Dependencies** — SCA (OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, Trivy).

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:

- **Comparisons** — drill the named patterns, the failure modes, and the recommended Java / framework idiom.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Storing JWTs in localStorage** = XSS-readable; httpOnly cookies are safer.
- **Log4Shell-grade incidents** — patch fast, mitigate by config when patch isn't possible.
- **Secrets** — never in code, never in env without a vault.
- **CSRF on stateless APIs** — disable; on cookie sessions — enable.
- **CSP** — most underused defence; even a basic policy stops most XSS classes.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"I'd treat input as hostile, parameterise every query, store passwords with BCrypt cost 12+, ship a CSP header, run SCA in CI, rotate secrets via vault, and review the OWASP Top 10 against the design before shipping."*
